y-m-51-01.title: If the values at the ends of an interval differ, does an inverse function exist?
y-m-51-01.topic: A quadratic function with a restricted domain and the existence of an inverse function
y-m-51-01.goal: Show with a counterexample why the criterion 'if the function values at both ends of the interval differ, it is a one-to-one correspondence' is not enough, and build several intervals on which an inverse function exists.
y-m-51-01.material: Let the domain of the function f(x)=x²-4x+3 be the interval a≤x≤b (a<b), and let the codomain be all the values f takes on that interval (the range). For the inverse function of f to exist, f must be a one-to-one correspondence on this interval. Sua said, "If the function values at both ends of the interval are different (f(a)≠f(b)), then f is a one-to-one correspondence on that interval." (Notation: f(x) is read 'f of x', and x² is read 'x squared'.)
y-m-51-01.thinking.0: Examine whether the criterion is a sufficient or a necessary condition
y-m-51-01.thinking.2: Make several intervals under a constraint
y-m-51-01.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-01.prereq.1: The graph and the axis of a quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (3rd-year middle school level)
y-m-51-01.prereq.2: Functions, one-to-one correspondence, and the condition for an inverse function to exist (Common Math level)
y-m-51-01.s.s1.prompt: Apply Sua's criterion to the interval 0≤x≤3. What is the most suitable judgment?
y-m-51-01.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate f(0), f(1), f(2), f(3) in order within the interval 0≤x≤3 and write them in a table.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, look for a place where the same function value appears twice.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.o.a: The end values f(0) and f(3) are different, so we can say f is a one-to-one correspondence on this interval
y-m-51-01.s.s1.r.a: You compared only the end values. You have not yet checked whether the values inside the interval are also different from each other.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.o.b: The end values are different, but inside the interval the values overlap, like f(1)=f(3), so we cannot say it is a one-to-one correspondence
y-m-51-01.s.s1.r.b: You looked not only at the end values but also at whether values inside the interval overlap.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.o.c: Whether the end values are different has nothing to do with being a one-to-one correspondence, so this criterion is useless from the start
y-m-51-01.s.s1.r.c: If it is a one-to-one correspondence, the end values must be different, so there is a connection. The problem is that 'being different' alone is not enough.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.o.d: Even if the domain is restricted to an interval, a quadratic function cannot be a one-to-one correspondence on any interval
y-m-51-01.s.s1.r.d: Think also about the case where the interval does not cross the vertex. On such an interval the values may not overlap.
y-m-51-01.s.s1.explain: f(0)=3 and f(3)=0, so the end values differ, but f(1)=0=f(3), so the same function value appears twice. 'The end values are different' is only a necessary condition for a one-to-one correspondence, not a sufficient one.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different intervals a≤x≤b (a<b, the length of the interval is 1 or more) on which an inverse function exists. The ends a and b of the interval may be real numbers.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick an interval and check with a few points whether f(x) keeps moving in only one direction as x increases within the interval.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the two ends of the interval with the position of the graph's axis of symmetry, and test three or four candidate intervals.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.var.a: Left end of the interval a
y-m-51-01.s.s2.var.b: Right end of the interval b
y-m-51-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a<b and the length is 1 or more.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.fail.c1: We need a<b and the length of the interval b-a must be 1 or more.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.ok.c2: On this interval the same function value does not appear twice.
y-m-51-01.s.s2.fail.c2: This interval contains two different x with the same function value. Find x1, x2 in the interval with f(x1)=f(x2).
y-m-51-01.s.s2.explain: Since f(x)=(x-2)²-1, f(x1)=f(x2) means x1=x2 or x1+x2=4. If the interval crosses x=2 (a<2<b), there are two points on both sides of 2 with sum 4 inside the interval, so the values overlap. So any interval with a≥2 or b≤2 can be an answer (e.g., [2,5], [-1,2], [3,4.5]).
y-m-51-01.s.s3.prompt: Answer Sua. Explain with a numerical example why Sua's criterion alone is not enough, and write in one sentence what shape an interval must have for an inverse function to exist.
y-m-51-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick an interval that passes Sua's criterion and yet has overlapping values, and make a table of its function values.
y-m-51-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write the sentence in the order 'e.g., ..., so ...'.
y-m-51-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the interval you gave, is it clear that the end values are different but the same function value appears twice?
y-m-51-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what position the interval must be in (its relation to the axis)?
y-m-51-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish that having different end values is necessary but not sufficient?
y-m-51-01.s.s3.model.0: On the interval 0≤x≤3, f(0)=3 and f(3)=0, so the end values differ, but f(1)=f(3)=0, so the same value appears twice. So it is not a one-to-one correspondence. The interval must be on only one side of the vertex x=2.
y-m-51-01.s.s3.model.1: Look at [1,4]: f(1)=0 and f(4)=3, so the end values differ, but f(1)=f(3), so the values overlap. The graph is symmetric left and right about x=2 as its axis, so the interval must not cross the axis.
y-m-51-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: You may write 'vertex' instead of the phrase 'axis x=2'.

y-m-51-02.title: If we change the order of composition, is it the same?
y-m-51-02.goal: Know that a few values of x for which swapping the order gave the same result cannot show that two functions are the same, and build for yourself the pairs of linear functions where the order does not matter and state the rule.
y-m-51-02.material: There are two functions f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x². Minsu said, "Composite functions are the same even if you swap the order. I tried it myself. If x=0, f(g(0))=1 and g(f(0))=1. If x=-2, f(g(-2))=9 and g(f(-2))=9. Both are the same, so f∘g=g∘f." (f∘g is read 'f composed with g', and g(x) is read 'g of x'.)
y-m-51-02.thinking.0: Review a claim generalized from a few matches
y-m-51-02.thinking.1: Make several examples under a constraint
y-m-51-02.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-02.prereq.2: The form of a linear function ax+b, and the meaning of two expressions being equal for all x
y-m-51-02.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable evaluation of Minsu's evidence?
y-m-51-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put in x=1 and calculate f(g(1)) and g(f(1)) separately.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write out both expressions directly and compare for how many x they become equal.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.o.a: They matched at both values, so it is enough to conclude f∘g=g∘f
y-m-51-02.s.s1.r.a: Two matching does not guarantee that they match for all x. You can test other x too.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.o.b: Swapping the order of composition always gives a different function, so Minsu's conclusion is impossible from the start
y-m-51-02.s.s1.r.b: There are pairs of functions that stay the same when the order is swapped. Being different for this pair does not mean all pairs are that way.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.o.c: Even if they are the same at x=0, -2, they must be the same for all x, so we must calculate other values like x=1 too
y-m-51-02.s.s1.r.c: You are looking at 'all x', not the number of matching values. You know that one other x can break the claim that the two functions are the same.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.o.d: The x tested were only 0 and a negative number, so the problem is that the signs were different, and if we check with a positive number it becomes the same
y-m-51-02.s.s1.r.d: It is not a problem of signs. Which x make them equal is decided by the expressions themselves. Calculate directly at the positive x=1.
y-m-51-02.s.s1.explain: f(g(x))=2x²+1 and g(f(x))=(2x+1)²=4x²+4x+1, and the two expressions are equal only at x=0, -2. At x=1 they are 3 and 9, so different. Even if they match at a few x, to be 'the same function' they must be equal for all x.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.prompt: Let f(x)=ax+b (a≠0) and g(x)=x+c. Make 3 different (a, b, c) such that f∘g=g∘f for all x and f and g are different functions.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) each in the form ax+(constant), and compare the constant parts.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put small integers into a and c and make a table to check whether the two constant parts are equal.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.var.a: Coefficient a of x in f
y-m-51-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The expressions of f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are the same for all x.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.fail.c2: When f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are each arranged in the form ax+(…), the constant terms differ.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.ok.c3: f and g are different functions.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.fail.c3: f and g ended up being the same function.
y-m-51-02.s.s2.explain: f(g(x))=a(x+c)+b=ax+ac+b and g(f(x))=ax+b+c. For the two expressions to be equal for all x, we need ac+b=b+c, that is, ac=c. So c=0 or a=1 works (e.g., a=3, b=2, c=0 or a=1, b=2, c=5). Both branches are answers.
y-m-51-02.s.s3.prompt: Looking at the examples you just made, write the rule for (a, b, c) such that f∘g=g∘f. And add when Minsu's statement is right only.
y-m-51-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write the two expressions you get by arranging f(g(x)) and g(f(x)).
y-m-51-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write the values of a and c of your three examples side by side and look for what they have in common.
y-m-51-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the rule fit all three examples you made?
y-m-51-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you find both branches (the case a=1 and the case c=0), or if you found only one, did you think that the other might exist?
y-m-51-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say 'right only sometimes' together with the reason?
y-m-51-02.s.s3.model.0: f∘g=ax+ac+b and g∘f=ax+b+c, so they are equal only when ac=c. So a=1 or c=0 is needed. Minsu's statement is right only in those cases.
y-m-51-02.s.s3.model.1: Since g is x+c, if c=0 then g(x)=x, so the order does not matter with any f, and if the slope of f is 1, both are translations, so the order does not matter. Minsu's statement is right only in these cases.
y-m-51-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that explained with a geometric reason without expanding the expressions.

y-m-51-03.title: How does the number of solutions change as we raise k?
y-m-51-03.topic: Intersections of the graph of a quadratic function with an absolute value and the line y=k
y-m-51-03.goal: Predict by transforming the graph (folding up) that the number of real roots of |f(x)|=k depends on the range of k, check your judgment against new information, and choose the k that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-51-03.material: f(x)=x²-2x-3=(x+1)(x-3) and g(x)=|f(x)|. We find how many different real roots the equation g(x)=k, that is, |f(x)|=k, has depending on the value of k. (|f(x)| is read 'the absolute value of f of x'.) Without drawing the graph directly, we build judgments by looking at the information one piece at a time.
y-m-51-03.thinking.1: Keep or revise a judgment with new information
y-m-51-03.thinking.2: Explain why the number changes at boundary values
y-m-51-03.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-03.prereq.1: The vertex and x-intercepts of a quadratic function, and the number of real roots of a quadratic equation
y-m-51-03.prereq.2: The fact that the graph of y=|f(x)| is the graph with the part where f(x)<0 folded up over the x-axis
y-m-51-03.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed step by step. Each time, predict the number of solutions, and after seeing new information, check your thinking.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.hint.0: Describe the graph of y=|f(x)| in words: where is it folded, and where is the highest point of the folded part?
y-m-51-03.s.s1.hint.1: As you raise the line y=k from below, count at how many heights the number of points meeting the graph changes.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.info: y=f(x) is a parabola opening upward, it meets the x-axis at x=-1 and x=3, and its vertex is (1, -4). The graph of y=|f(x)| is the curve on the interval where f(x) is negative (-1<x<3) folded up over the x-axis.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many different real roots does |f(x)|=1 have?
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.after: f(x)=1 is x²-2x-4=0, which has two different real roots, and f(x)=-1 is x²-2x-2=0, which has two different real roots, so there are 4 in all. The folded graph has a W shape, so y=1 meets it in four places.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You may have thought only of f(x)=1. Count also the points where the folded part meets y=1.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You counted the solutions of both f(x)=1 and f(x)=-1.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is a special height at which there are 3. Check whether that height is the current 1.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You may have looked at only one vertex. Count all the points where y=1 meets the graph.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.info: The folded part is a parabola opening downward with vertex (1, 4). Think of raising the line y=k from below, from k=1 up to k=3.9.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Even if k is raised from 1 to 3.9, does the number of solutions stay at 4?
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.after: At k=3.9 too, f(x)=3.9 and f(x)=-3.9 each have two different real roots, so there are 4. Before reaching the vertex height 4, it is right to keep your first judgment as it is.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It stays. Until it reaches the vertex height 4, it stays 4
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You kept your first judgment, matching it with the new information (the vertex height 4).
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: As it gets close to 3.9, the solutions drop one at a time and become 3
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It becomes 3 when the line touches exactly the vertex height. 3.9 is not yet that height.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The higher you raise it, the fewer solutions, and in the end it becomes 2
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought the solutions drop right away when raised. Count again how many points meet the W shape while the height is below 4.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The higher you raise it, the more points meet, becoming 5 or more
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Think about the most points a curve and a line can meet at one height in this graph.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Solving directly: for k=4, f(x)=4 gives x=1±2√2 (2 solutions) and f(x)=-4 gives (x-1)²=0, so x=1 (1 solution), 3 in all. For k=5, f(x)=5 gives x=4, -2 (2 solutions) and f(x)=-5 has a negative discriminant so no real roots, so 2. If k=0, x=-1, 3 (2 solutions), and if k<0, |f(x)|≥0 so there are no solutions.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most suitable summary of the number of solutions by the value of k?
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The number changes separately at the boundary values k=0 and k=4, and between and outside them it stays constant at 4 and 2 respectively. The first prediction (4 for k=1) extended to the whole of 0<k<4.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You missed that at k=4 the folded vertex and the line touch at one point.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You summarized even that the number changes separately at the boundaries k=0 and k=4.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You missed that when k=0 there are two x-intercepts (-1, 3).
y-m-51-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Count again how many points meet above the folded part when k is greater than 4.
y-m-51-03.s.s1.reflect: With what information did you keep the prediction you made at first with k=1, and with what information did you come to revise it by interval?
y-m-51-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different k for which |f(x)|=k has exactly 4 different real roots. (k is a real number)
y-m-51-03.s.s2.hint.0: Find the interval with 4 among the numbers by interval you summarized in the earlier step.
y-m-51-03.s.s2.hint.1: Leave out the two boundary values from the candidates and choose a value between them.
y-m-51-03.s.s2.ok.c1: For this k, |f(x)|=k has 4 different real roots.
y-m-51-03.s.s2.fail.c1: For this k, the number of real roots is not 4. Compare with the heights 0 and 4.
y-m-51-03.s.s2.explain: If 0<k<4, f(x)=k and f(x)=-k each have two different real roots, so 4 in all. Any k in this range is an answer.
y-m-51-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain, connecting it to the shape of the graph, why there are 3 solutions only when k=4, and also write the numbers before and after k=4 (for 0<k<4 and for k>4).
y-m-51-03.s.s3.hint.0: Copy over, as they are, the numbers for k=4 and for the intervals before and after it from the summary table in the earlier step.
y-m-51-03.s.s3.hint.1: Describe in words how the highest point of the folded part and the line meet.
y-m-51-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does it include that at k=4 the line touches the vertex of the folded part?
y-m-51-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the numbers for 0<k<4 and k>4 correctly?
y-m-51-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain 'why it is 3' with the shape, not just the number?
y-m-51-03.s.s3.model.0: The height of the vertex of the folded part is 4, so at k=4 the line touches that vertex, and adding the two points on both sides makes 3. If 0<k<4 it is 4, and if k>4 it is 2.
y-m-51-03.s.s3.model.1: y=|f(x)| is a W shape and the height of the middle peak is 4. When the line touches the peak exactly, it meets at one point there, so 3 in all; lower than that it is 4, and higher it meets only at the two outer points, so 2.
y-m-51-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explained with the analogy of a W shape.

y-m-51-04.title: Which bundle of information fixes a rational function to one?
y-m-51-04.topic: Information needed to fix the graph of a rational function
y-m-51-04.goal: Sort out the information that fixes the rational function y=k/(x-p)+q to one and the information that does not, and notice impossible conditions such as a point on an asymptote.
y-m-51-04.material: We want to fix the graph of the rational function y=k/(x-p)+q (k≠0). The asymptotes are the two lines x=p and y=q. Among the following five bundles of conditions, choose all those whose conditions alone fix the graph to exactly one. (k/(x-p) is read 'k over x minus p'.)
y-m-51-04.thinking.0: Count the unknowns and the conditions
y-m-51-04.thinking.2: Make different examples when information is lacking
y-m-51-04.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-04.prereq.1: The asymptotes (x=p, y=q) of the rational function y=k/(x-p)+q
y-m-51-04.prereq.2: Setting up an expression by substituting the coordinates of a point
y-m-51-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the bundles of conditions that fix the graph to exactly one. (If there is no such graph or more than one, it is not 'fixed'.)
y-m-51-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each bundle of conditions, count how many values are still unknown (k, p, q) and compare with the number of equations the conditions make.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.hint.1: For bundles that give a point, substitute that point into y=k/(x-p)+q and write the equation.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.o.a: The asymptotes are x=2 and y=1
y-m-51-04.s.s1.r.a: Two asymptotes only fix p and q. k is still left.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.o.b: The asymptote is y=1 and it passes through the point (4, 3)
y-m-51-04.s.s1.r.b: The unknowns p and k are left but there is only one equation. Check whether k can be matched for each value of p.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.o.c: The asymptotes are x=2 and y=1 and it passes through the point (4, 3)
y-m-51-04.s.s1.r.c: Only k is left, and one equation fixes k. This is a judgment made by matching the number of unknowns with the number of equations.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.o.d: The asymptotes are x=2 and y=1 and it passes through the point (2, 5)
y-m-51-04.s.s1.r.d: The point is on an asymptote. First think about whether the graph can pass through that point.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.o.e: The asymptote is x=2 and it passes through the two points (4, 3) and (3, 5)
y-m-51-04.s.s1.r.e: The unknowns k and q are left and there are two equations. Solve to see whether the two equations fix both.
y-m-51-04.s.s1.explain: c gives just one, 4/(x-2)+1, and e also gives one graph with k=4, q=1. For a, k is free, and for b, k=2(4-p) is matched for each p, so there are infinitely many (p=4 is excluded because the point would be on the asymptote), and d has a point on an asymptote so there is no such graph at all.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.prompt: We want y=k/(x-2)+1, whose asymptotes are x=2 and y=1, to pass through a point (a, b). Make 3 points (a, b), with a and b integers and k positive, that give different graphs (different k).
y-m-51-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put the point (a, b) into the expression and write k in terms of a and b.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.hint.1: Test two or three points and check whether k comes out different.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The point is not on an asymptote.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The point is on an asymptote (x=2 or y=1). The graph cannot pass through such a point.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The k of the graph through this point is positive.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.fail.c3: If it passes through this point, k is 0 or less. Check the sign of k.
y-m-51-04.s.s2.explain: Substituting the point (a,b) into y=k/(x-2)+1 gives k=(a-2)(b-1). For (4,3), k=4; for (3,3), k=2; for (5,2), k=3, so different graphs come out. Points that give the same k (e.g., (4,3) and (6,2)) are the same graph, so count them as one.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.prompt: Explain why condition B alone (the asymptote is y=1 and it passes through the point (4, 3)) does not fix the graph to one, by showing the expressions of two different graphs that satisfy the conditions.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.hint.0: The asymptote y=1 means q=1. Pick a p and substitute the point (4,3) to find k.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.hint.1: Change p to another value and do it once more, and compare the two results.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check by substitution that both expressions you gave pass through the point (4, 3) and have the asymptote y=1?
y-m-51-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that k also changes when the value of p changes?
y-m-51-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about p=4 not being allowed because the point would be on the asymptote?
y-m-51-04.s.s3.model.0: If p=3 and k=2, then y=2/(x-3)+1 passes through (4,3), and if p=2 and k=4, then y=4/(x-2)+1 also passes through (4,3). The asymptote y=1 is the same but the graphs differ, so it is not fixed to one.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.model.1: Both the case k=2, p=3 and the case k=8, p=0 are y=k/(x-p)+1 that pass through the point (4,3). So several different graphs are possible.
y-m-51-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It gave y=8/x+1 with p=0 as an example.

y-m-51-05.title: Check a working that found the minimum within an interval
y-m-51-05.topic: Maximum and minimum of a quadratic function with a restricted domain
y-m-51-05.goal: Find the error in a working for the minimum of a quadratic function on a restricted interval that overlooked the case where the vertex is outside the interval, and build several intervals on which the maximum and minimum take given values.
y-m-51-05.material: This is a problem of finding the maximum and minimum of the function f(x)=x²-4x+1 when the domain is 3≤x≤6. Junho's working is as follows. (x² is read 'x squared', and ≤ is read 'less than or equal to'.)
y-m-51-05.thinking.0: Find where the error in the working is
y-m-51-05.thinking.2: Make several intervals under a constraint
y-m-51-05.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-05.prereq.1: The vertex and graph shape of a quadratic function, and the maximum and minimum on a restricted interval (3rd-year middle school to Common Math level)
y-m-51-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Junho's working whose basis is wrong.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one whether the value of x used in each line is inside the domain 3≤x≤6.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.hint.1: Mark 3, 6, and the x-coordinate of the vertex on a number line and check their positions.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.line.1: The vertex of the graph is (2, -3), so the minimum is -3.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.line.2: f(3)=-2 and f(6)=13, so the maximum is 13.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the minimum is -3 and the maximum is 13.
y-m-51-05.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the root error. The x-coordinate of the vertex, 2, is not in the domain 3≤x≤6, so -3 does not actually occur on this interval. Line 4 is a conclusion that carries over that error. The calculations in lines 1 and 3 are right. On this interval the graph goes up toward the right, so the minimum is f(3)=-2 at x=3.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.prompt: Looking at the same function f(x)=x²-4x+1 on an interval a≤x≤b (a<b), make 3 different intervals on which the minimum is -3 and the maximum is 6.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.hint.0: Decide where the interval must pass for the x that gives the minimum -3 to be inside the interval.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find the x with f(x)=6 and think about whether one end of the interval must be that value.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.var.a: Left end of the interval a
y-m-51-05.s.s2.var.b: Right end of the interval b
y-m-51-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The minimum -3 occurs within the interval.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.fail.c2: On this interval the minimum is not -3. Check whether the x that gives the minimum is inside the interval.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The maximum within the interval is 6.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The maximum within the interval is not 6. Compare the function values at the two ends of the interval.
y-m-51-05.s.s2.explain: Since f(x)=(x-2)²-3, if x=2 is in the interval, the minimum is -3. And the higher of the two ends of the interval gives the maximum, and the x with f(x)=6 are -1 and 5. So intervals with a=-1 and 2≤b≤5, or with b=5 and -1≤a≤2, are all answers (e.g., [-1,2], [-1,5], [0,5], [2,5]).
y-m-51-05.s.s3.prompt: Tell Junho where it went wrong, and write the correct minimum on this interval and the reason.
y-m-51-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write in a sentence whether the x=2 that Junho used is inside the domain 3≤x≤6.
y-m-51-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check with a few points how the function value moves as x grows within the interval.
y-m-51-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the reason that the vertex is outside the interval with the numbers of the interval?
y-m-51-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also say at which x the correct minimum occurs?
y-m-51-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about under what condition the generalization 'the minimum is always at the vertex' is right?
y-m-51-05.s.s3.model.0: The vertex x=2 is not in the domain 3≤x≤6, so -3 can't actually occur. On the interval, the minimum is -2 at x=3.
y-m-51-05.s.s3.model.1: The graph is lowest at x=2, but that point is outside the range. Inside the range it goes up toward the right, so the minimum is -2 at the left end x=3.
y-m-51-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: Even if expressions such as 'range' or 'x=2' differ, it is the same content.

y-m-51-06.title: Translation and reflection: if we change the order, is it the same?
y-m-51-06.topic: Composition of a translation and a reflection in the line y=x
y-m-51-06.goal: Examine whether a result that looked the same regardless of order in one example can be generalized, and make translations for yourself where the point stays the same when the order is changed, to find the condition.
y-m-51-06.material: Two moves are applied to a point A(a, b) on the coordinate plane. The translation T is 'by p in the direction of the x-axis and by q in the direction of the y-axis', and the reflection R is the reflection in the line y=x. For A(1, 4), p=3, q=3, Seoyun checked that both 'T then R' and 'R then T' give the point (7, 4), and said, "Even if you change the order, the result is always the same." (R is 'the move that swaps the coordinates'. y=x is read 'y equals x'.)
y-m-51-06.thinking.0: Check a generalization from one example
y-m-51-06.thinking.1: Discover the condition with examples you make yourself
y-m-51-06.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-06.prereq.2: Reflection in the line y=x: (a,b)→(b,a) (Common Math level)
y-m-51-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most suitable evaluation of Seoyun's check and conclusion.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.hint.0: Notice that p and q are the same number in Seoyun's example, and pick one case where p and q are different.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.hint.1: For the point A(1, 4), calculate the results of the two orders as coordinates and compare them.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.o.a: The same result came out once, so we can regard it as the same for all points and all moves, regardless of order
y-m-51-06.s.s1.r.a: You regarded it as 'always' from just one match. The case where the move distances are changed has not been checked yet.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.o.b: It matched because point A=(1, 4) was special, and if A is changed to another point it will differ
y-m-51-06.s.s1.r.b: It could be the sizes p and q of the move that decide the result, not the coordinates of A. Tell apart whether you tried changing A or changing p and q.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.o.c: A translation and a reflection are different kinds of transformation, so comparing the order itself is meaningless
y-m-51-06.s.s1.r.c: Comparing the results by changing the order is meaningful. There are also cases where changing it gives a different point.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.o.d: It is just one example that holds, so we should do the same calculation again with another move with p≠q
y-m-51-06.s.s1.r.d: You took one example as the basis while also thinking about which values to change.
y-m-51-06.s.s1.explain: It matched in the special case p=q=3. 'T then R' gives (b+q, a+p) and 'R then T' gives (b+p, a+q), so they can differ unless p=q (e.g., for A(1,4), p=3, q=0, they are (4,4) and (7,1)).
y-m-51-06.s.s2.prompt: Make moves for which the results of the two orders ('T then R' and 'R then T') are the same point. The move must actually happen ((p,q)≠(0,0)). Make 3 with different moves (p, q), and choose the point A(a, b) freely.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a point, write the coordinates after moving it in each of the two orders, and compare the two coordinates side by side.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.hint.1: In the examples that came out the same, write p and q side by side and look for something in common.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.var.p: Movement p in the x-axis direction
y-m-51-06.s.s2.var.q: Movement q in the y-axis direction
y-m-51-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The results of the two orders are the same point.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The results of the two orders are different points. Calculate and compare the coordinates of 'T then R' and 'R then T'.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.fail.c2: If p and q are both 0, there is no move.
y-m-51-06.s.s2.explain: 'T then R' is (a,b)→(a+p,b+q)→(b+q,a+p), and 'R then T' is (a,b)→(b,a)→(b+p,a+q). For them to be equal, q=p is needed. So a move that shifts by the same amount in the x-axis and y-axis directions does not depend on order (any point A will do), and if p≠q they differ.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to Seoyun. Write the condition for which moves Seoyun's statement is right, and give one example with numbers where the result changes when the order is different.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.hint.0: Change p and q in Seoyun's example to be different from each other and write the results of the two orders as coordinates.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.hint.1: For the three moves you made, write p and q side by side and write what they have in common in a sentence.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state the condition clearly, such as 'when p and q are equal'?
y-m-51-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the results of both orders in the examples you gave?
y-m-51-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you not completely deny Seoyun's statement but separate the cases where it is right from those where it is wrong?
y-m-51-06.s.s3.model.0: It is the same only when p and q are equal, that is, when p=q. For example, if A(1,4) is moved with p=3, q=0, the results of the two orders differ, (4,4) and (7,1), so Seoyun's statement is right only for some.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.model.1: The direction of the move is the same as the direction of y=x, so when shifting by the same amount in the x-axis and y-axis directions (e.g., 2 and 2) the order doesn't matter. But if you shift in only one direction like (3,0), the result differs.
y-m-51-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that unpacked p=q in terms of direction.

y-m-51-07.title: Are the intersections with the inverse function always on y=x?
y-m-51-07.topic: Intersections of the graph of a function and the graph of its inverse function
y-m-51-07.goal: Do not be convinced of the claim 'the intersections of f and f⁻¹ are always on y=x' by the evidence of one function; make a counterexample with a decreasing function and explain to a friend how it differs from an increasing function.
y-m-51-07.material: Minjae said, "The points where y=f(x) and its inverse function y=f⁻¹(x) meet are always on the line y=x. Because the two graphs are symmetric about y=x." As evidence, he solved f(x)=x³ (the domain is all real numbers) and showed that the intersections (-1,-1), (0,0), (1,1) are all on y=x. (f⁻¹ is read 'f inverse'.)
y-m-51-07.thinking.0: Judge the scope of the evidence
y-m-51-07.thinking.2: State the condition for it to hold (an increasing function)
y-m-51-07.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-07.prereq.1: The meaning of an inverse function and the relation between the graphs of f and f⁻¹
y-m-51-07.prereq.2: The graph shapes of the power functions x³ and -x³
y-m-51-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most suitable evaluation of Minjae's evidence.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether f(x)=x³ is increasing or decreasing, and recall one example of another shape (a decreasing function).
y-m-51-07.s.s1.hint.1: For an intersection (a,b) to be on both f and f⁻¹, both (a,b) and (b,a) must be on f. Write this meaning as an expression.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.o.a: He checked only one function, so he should also test with a function that is not increasing
y-m-51-07.s.s1.r.a: You thought of the point that before extending the result of one function to all functions, you must test other kinds.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.o.b: Three intersections came out, so it can be regarded as having checked enough cases
y-m-51-07.s.s1.r.b: Several points coming out for the same function is a check on one function. Whether it is the same for other functions is a separate matter.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.o.c: Graphs symmetric about y=x must have their intersections on y=x, so the proof is already finished
y-m-51-07.s.s1.r.c: Examine whether there are no cases where two symmetric graphs meet outside y=x. Even when symmetric, two points facing each other can both be intersections.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.o.d: A cubic function does not have an inverse function, so this evidence cannot be used in the first place
y-m-51-07.s.s1.r.d: f(x)=x³ is a one-to-one correspondence on all real numbers, so it has an inverse function. Whether the evidence can be used and whether it is sufficient are separate matters.
y-m-51-07.s.s1.explain: f(x)=x³ is an increasing function. For increasing functions the intersections are on y=x, but for decreasing functions it may not necessarily be so. Checking one function does not guarantee the whole claim.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.prompt: For f(x)=-x³ (the domain is all real numbers, a one-to-one correspondence), find points (a, b) that are on both the graph of f and the graph of f⁻¹ but are not on y=x. Make 2 different points.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write separately the expression for (a, b) being on f and the expression for it being on f⁻¹ (the expression with a and b swapped).
y-m-51-07.s.s2.hint.1: Put small integers like -1, 0, 1 into a to find b and check whether the second expression holds.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The point (a,b) is not on y=-x³.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The point (b,a) is also on f, so (a,b) is also on f⁻¹.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.fail.c2: (b,a) is not on f, so (a,b) is not on f⁻¹.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.ok.c3: This point is not on y=x.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.fail.c3: This point is on y=x. It is not a counterexample.
y-m-51-07.s.s2.explain: If (a,b) is on f, then b=-a³, and if it is on f⁻¹, then (b,a) is on f, so a=-b³. From the two expressions, a⁹=a, so a=0, 1, -1, and the only ones not on y=x are the two points (1,-1) and (-1,1).
y-m-51-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to send to Minjae. Show concretely the function for which Minjae's claim breaks and its intersections, and add for what kind of function the claim is right.
y-m-51-07.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one of the points you made in the earlier step and substitute directly to check whether it is a point on f and whether (b,a) is a point on f.
y-m-51-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write the reply in the order 'counterexample → the case where it is right → a one-line summary'.
y-m-51-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with two expressions that the point you gave is really a point on f and also a point on f⁻¹?
y-m-51-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you point out in one line the case where the claim is right (an increasing function)?
y-m-51-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you show the evidence concretely without blaming Minjae?
y-m-51-07.s.s3.model.0: For f(x)=-x³, (1,-1) is on f, and f(-1)=1, so it is also on f⁻¹. But it is not a point on y=x. The claim is right for increasing functions, but it can break if f is decreasing.
y-m-51-07.s.s3.model.1: If it is an increasing function the intersections are on y=x, but a decreasing function like -x³ also meets outside y=x, as at (-1,1) and (1,-1). Because they are symmetric, you must not conclude that they meet on y=x.
y-m-51-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that also mentioned that it holds for increasing functions.

y-m-51-08.title: What more is needed to fix the tangent line to one?
y-m-51-08.topic: The condition for a quadratic function and a line to be tangent
y-m-51-08.goal: Know that for a line y=mx+n tangent to a parabola, the tangency condition is only one relation between the slope and the y-intercept, and judge whether extra information fixes the line to one (one, two, or none).
y-m-51-08.material: We want to find the line y=mx+n tangent to the parabola y=x²-2x+3. (Being tangent means meeting the parabola at only one point.) The tangency condition alone does not fix the line to one. In addition to the tangency condition, which of the information below fixes the line to exactly one? (x²-2x+3 is read 'x squared minus 2x plus 3'.)
y-m-51-08.thinking.0: Count the unknowns and the conditions
y-m-51-08.thinking.1: Find out that the number of solutions differs by case
y-m-51-08.thinking.2: Make several lines under a constraint
y-m-51-08.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-08.prereq.1: The number of real roots of a quadratic equation and its relation to the coefficients
y-m-51-08.prereq.2: The intersections of the line y=mx+n and the parabola are the roots of the equation made from the two expressions
y-m-51-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information that, in addition to the tangency condition, fix the line to exactly one.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.hint.0: Combine the expressions of the line and the parabola into an equation in x, and write how many solutions that equation must have for them to meet at only one point.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.hint.1: Put the information of each option into the relation between m and n, and check one by one how many solutions the remaining unknown has.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.o.a: The y-intercept of the line is 2
y-m-51-08.s.s1.r.a: If the y-intercept is fixed, a quadratic expression in the slope comes out. Look back at whether you checked how many solutions that expression has.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.o.b: The slope of the line is 1
y-m-51-08.s.s1.r.b: If the slope is fixed, the y-intercept is found as one value from the tangency condition.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.o.c: The line passes through the point (1, 1)
y-m-51-08.s.s1.r.c: The condition of passing through a point lets you rewrite n in terms of m. Then check how many solutions the expression in m has.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.o.d: The y-intercept of the line is 3
y-m-51-08.s.s1.r.d: If the y-intercept is 3, the line passes through the point (0, 3) on the parabola. Check with the discriminant how many solutions there are in this case.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.o.e: The y-intercept of the line is 4
y-m-51-08.s.s1.r.e: If the y-intercept is 4, compare with the parabola where the point the line passes through is. You must first check whether such a line exists.
y-m-51-08.s.s1.explain: The discriminant of x²-(m+2)x+3-n=0, made by combining the parabola and the line y=mx+n, must be 0, so (m+2)²=4(3-n). With slope 1, n=3/4, one; with y-intercept 3, (m+2)²=0, so m=-2, one. With y-intercept 2, m=0 or -4, two; passing through the point (1,1), m=2 or -2, two; with y-intercept 4, (m+2)²=-4, so there is no real m.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.prompt: Among the tangent lines y=mx+n, make 3 different lines whose slope m is an integer. (n is a real number)
y-m-51-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the relation between m and n you got in the earlier step, and put integers into m to find n.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.hint.1: Put the (m, n) you found into the system of the first two expressions and check once more that there is one solution.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The slope m must be an integer.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.ok.c2: This line is tangent to the parabola.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.fail.c2: This line is not tangent. Calculate the discriminant of the combined quadratic equation.
y-m-51-08.s.s2.explain: The discriminant of x²-(m+2)x+3-n=0 must be 0, so (m+2)²=4(3-n). Once an integer m is chosen, n is fixed to one, so (0,2), (-2,3), (2,-1), (-4,2), (1,3/4), and so on are all answers.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.prompt: Explain in words why there are two tangent lines when the y-intercept is 2. You may explain by calculating the expressions, or by the position of the point (0, 2) and the parabola.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.hint.0: If the y-intercept is 2, put n=2 into the relation between m and n and write the expression for m.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many solutions that expression has.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show that there are two lines with numbers or expressions (m=0, m=-4, etc.)?
y-m-51-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Whether you solved with the discriminant or looked at the position, did your reasoning continue to the end?
y-m-51-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you explain separately why there is only one when the y-intercept is 3?
y-m-51-08.s.s3.model.0: If n=2, the discriminant gives (m+2)²=4, so m=0 or -4, two values, so there are two lines. So the y-intercept alone does not fix it to one.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.model.1: The point (0,2) is outside, below the parabola, and from a point outside you can draw 2 tangent lines. So y-intercept 2 gives 2 lines.
y-m-51-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that explained with position instead of the discriminant.

y-m-51-09.title: Per-minute fee and interval fee: when is which one cheaper?
y-m-51-09.topic: Comparing a linear function and a staircase-shaped function
y-m-51-09.goal: Check a conclusion drawn from comparing only a few usage times, and show with a counterexample and an explanation that the comparison result can change by interval because of the staircase structure of the interval fee.
y-m-51-09.material: A shared bicycle service offers two fee plans. The usage time t is a natural number in minutes and is charged in 1-minute units. Plan A is 40원 per minute, so the fee is 40t원. Plan B is 1000원 up to the first 30 minutes, and after 30 minutes, 500원 is added for every 10 minutes (even if it is less than 10 minutes, you pay one more time). For example, 31 minutes is 1500원, 40 minutes is also 1500원, and 41 minutes is 2000원. A student calculated t=20, 45, 60 minutes and said, "A was cheaper all three times, so there is no time when B is cheaper than A."
y-m-51-09.thinking.0: Find out the risk of generalizing from samples
y-m-51-09.thinking.1: Calculate a function with rounding up
y-m-51-09.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-09.prereq.1: The graph of the linear function y=ax and calculating values of a function with round-up (ceil)
y-m-51-09.prereq.2: Reading the interval of solutions of an inequality
y-m-51-09.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable evaluation of the student's evidence and conclusion?
y-m-51-09.s.s1.hint.0: Pick times before and after where the fee of B changes like a staircase (30 minutes, 40 minutes, etc.) and calculate both fees.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table comparing the fees of A and B for t=25, 28, 35, 39.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.o.a: A was cheaper all three times, so we can regard it as there being no time anywhere when B is cheaper than A
y-m-51-09.s.s1.r.a: You extended the result at three times to all times. You did not check near the points where the fee changes.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.o.b: B's fee changes by interval and is not a line, so comparing the two plans is impossible
y-m-51-09.s.s1.r.b: Even if it is not a line, you can calculate the fee for each time and compare. You can just check each interval separately.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.o.c: A is a line and B is staircase-shaped, so the longer the time, the cheaper B surely becomes
y-m-51-09.s.s1.r.c: The shape of the graph alone does not decide which is cheaper. Compare the per-minute fee, which corresponds to the slope.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.o.d: Three times alone cannot tell the whole story, so we should also calculate before and after 30 minutes where the fee changes
y-m-51-09.s.s1.r.d: You thought of both that the sample is small and where else to look.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.o.e: The times were far apart from each other, so the check was wrong, and if they were close times the conclusion would be right
y-m-51-09.s.s1.r.e: It is not a problem of spacing. Which times you pick is what matters. Calculate close times directly.
y-m-51-09.s.s1.explain: At t=20, 45, 60 A was cheaper, but it changes if you look near 30 minutes where the fee changes (e.g., for t=28, A is 1120원 and B is 1000원). You cannot say 'always' from a few representative values.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different usage times t (minutes) for which B is cheaper than A. (t is a natural number)
y-m-51-09.s.s2.hint.0: At 30 minutes or less, B's fee is constant at 1000원. Find the times when A's fee is greater than 1000원.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.hint.1: From 31 to 40 minutes, B's fee is constant at 1500원. Find the times before A's fee exceeds 1500원.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.fail.c1: t must be a natural number (minutes) that is 1 or more.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.ok.c2: At this time, B's fee is cheaper than A's fee.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time, B is not cheaper than A. Calculate the two fees separately and compare.
y-m-51-09.s.s2.explain: B is cheaper at t=26 to 30 minutes and t=38 to 40 minutes. For example, for t=28, A is 1120원 and B is 1000원, and for t=39, A is 1560원 and B is 1500원. At t=25 and t=50 the two fees are equal.
y-m-51-09.s.s3.prompt: Summarize, writing the range of usage time with numbers, how it would be good to choose between the two plans. (If there are times with equal fees, say so.)
y-m-51-09.s.s3.hint.0: List in order from the smallest the times you found in the earlier step when B is cheaper.
y-m-51-09.s.s3.hint.1: Also calculate the two fees just before and after the times you listed (e.g., 25, 31, 37, 41, 50) and check whether they are equal.
y-m-51-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write exactly the range of times when B is cheaper (26 to 30 minutes, 38 to 40 minutes) and the times with equal fees (25 minutes, 50 minutes)?
y-m-51-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that A is cheaper at the other times?
y-m-51-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish whether the boundary values are included (or less / less than)?
y-m-51-09.s.s3.model.0: B is cheaper from 26 to 30 minutes and from 38 to 40 minutes, and they are equal at 25 minutes and 50 minutes. At other times A is cheaper, so for most times it is better to choose A.
y-m-51-09.s.s3.model.1: A is cheaper at 25 minutes or less, 31 to 37 minutes, 41 to 49 minutes, and 51 minutes or more, and B is cheaper only at 26 to 30 minutes and 38 to 40 minutes. At 25 minutes and 50 minutes the amounts are equal.
y-m-51-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that listed the intervals where A is cheaper.

y-m-51-10.title: Check a working that read the signs of the coefficients from a description of the graph
y-m-51-10.topic: Reading the signs of the coefficients from the shape of a quadratic function's graph
y-m-51-10.goal: Find the error in an inequality calculation in a working that reads the signs of a, b, c from the shape of the graph, find out the cases where information is lacking, and then build quadratic functions that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-51-10.material: This is a description in words of the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c. This graph opens downward (convex upward), its vertex is to the upper right of the y-axis (the first quadrant), it meets the y-axis at the positive part (above the origin), and it meets the x-axis at two different points. Hyunwoo read the signs of a, b, c, and the discriminant from this description as shown below. (ax² is read 'a x squared', and -b/(2a) is read 'minus b over 2a'.)
y-m-51-10.thinking.0: Find the error in the working
y-m-51-10.thinking.2: Make several expressions under a constraint
y-m-51-10.prereq.0: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty label in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied the prerequisites below.
y-m-51-10.prereq.1: The graph shape of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c and its axis x=-b/(2a)
y-m-51-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Hyunwoo's working whose basis is wrong.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.hint.0: For the inequality -b/(2a)>0 in line 3, put a negative number (e.g., a=-1) into a and check what sign b must have.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.hint.1: Make one quadratic function with a=-1 and the axis on the right (e.g., x=1) and read the sign of b directly.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.line.0: The graph is convex upward, so a<0.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.line.1: The y-coordinate of the point where it meets the y-axis is positive, so c>0.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.line.2: The axis x=-b/(2a) is to the right of the y-axis, so -b/(2a)>0, and since a<0, b<0.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.line.3: It meets the x-axis at two different points, so b²-4ac>0.
y-m-51-10.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. In -b/(2a)>0, 2a is negative, so multiplying both sides by 2a reverses the inequality sign, giving -b<0, that is, b>0. (When a<0 and the axis is on the right, b is positive.) Lines 1, 2, and 4 are right.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.prompt: When we only know the information that the graph is convex upward (a<0) and meets the y-axis at the positive part (c>0), what is the sign of b?
y-m-51-10.s.s2.hint.0: Set a=-1, c=1, put 3, -3, 0 into b to get three expressions, and compare them by the shape of the graph.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check that all three expressions are convex upward and have y-intercept 1.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.o.a: b is necessarily positive. Because it is convex upward and the y-intercept is positive
y-m-51-10.s.s2.r.a: You concluded that b is positive from a<0 and c>0 alone. Check whether you can make an example where b is negative.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.o.b: b is necessarily negative. Because it is convex upward and the y-intercept is positive
y-m-51-10.s.s2.r.b: You concluded that b is negative from a<0 and c>0 alone. Check whether you can make an example where b is positive.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.o.c: It cannot be decided, and we need to know more about which side of the y-axis the axis is on
y-m-51-10.s.s2.r.c: You made examples directly to check whether the given information fixes b, and even pointed out what more information is needed.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.o.d: b is necessarily 0. Because it is convex upward and the y-intercept is positive
y-m-51-10.s.s2.r.d: b=0 is the special case where the axis coincides with the y-axis. Check whether the information contains such a condition.
y-m-51-10.s.s2.explain: y=-x²+3x+1 (b>0), y=-x²-3x+1 (b<0), and y=-x²+1 (b=0) all satisfy a<0, c>0. The sign of b is decided by which side of the y-axis the axis x=-b/(2a) is on.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.prompt: For a quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c that is convex upward with the x-coordinate of its vertex greater than 1 and less than 2 (1<x<2), make 3 different integer triples (a, b, c) with c>0. (|a|, |b|, |c| are at most 9)
y-m-51-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write the x-coordinate of the vertex using a and b, and write as an inequality the condition for it to lie between 1 and 2.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.hint.1: Fix one a and find the integer values b can take.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, and c are integers and it is convex upward.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be a negative integer, and b and c must be integers too.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.ok.c2: The size of each coefficient is at most 9.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.ok.c4: The x-coordinate of the vertex is between 1 and 2.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.fail.c4: The x-coordinate of the vertex, -b/(2a), is not between 1 and 2. Check the position of the axis with the expression.
y-m-51-10.s.s3.explain: The axis x=-b/(2a)=b/(2|a|), so 1<b/(2|a|)<2, that is, 2|a|<b<4|a|. If a=-1, then b=3; if a=-2, then b=5, 6, 7; if a=-3, then b=7 to 11 (at most 9). c just needs to be positive, and if it is convex upward and c>0, it meets the x-axis at two different points.
